notes: Attorney General's Reference on unduly lenient s18 wounding sentence; aggravating and mitigating features and substituted sentence are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: knife wounding sentence increased from 3 years 9 months to 6 years
key_facts: The offender was convicted at Preston Crown Court of wounding with intent after stabbing the victim twice with a concealed 7-inch knife during a dispute over money at the victim's home.
The victim suffered neck and head wounds requiring stitches, permanent scarring, and lasting psychological effects.
Judge Badley sentenced the offender to 3 years 9 months' imprisonment after trial.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient, citing premeditation, use of a knife, attack in the victim's home, and sustained violence to vulnerable body parts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's Reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 following conviction and sentence at crown court.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer granted; sentence of 3 years 9 months quashed and substituted with 6 years' imprisonment, taking double jeopardy into account.
enrichment.ratio: A very serious section 18 wounding with intent involving premeditated retrieval of a knife, disarming of the victim, and repeated stabs to the neck and head in the victim's home warranted, after trial, a sentence of at least 7 years; allowing for double jeopardy on reference, 6 years was appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether the original sentence for wounding with intent was unduly lenient
Appropriate sentencing bracket for serious knife wounding with intent after trial
Weight to be given to aggravating features including premeditation and domestic setting
Application of double jeopardy in Attorney General's References

Attorney-General's Reference Nos 59, 60 and 63 of 1998 [1999] 2 Cr App R(S) 128
Attorney-General's Reference No 52 of 2001 (R v Lamoon) [2001] EWCA Crim 1906
Attorney-General's Reference No 18 of 2002 (R v Hughes) [2003] Cr App R(S) 35

notes: Trial ruling on CPR 32.13 witness statement inspection and CPR 5.4 statements of case access in a heavily reported cohabitee property dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Cox v Jones: media inspection of witness statements and pleadings at trial
key_facts: Cox v Jones concerned ownership of properties following the break-up of an engaged couple's relationship.
During trial the defendant withdrew factual 'gold-digger' and relationship allegations that had not been put in cross-examination; parts of the defence were struck out.
The Times sought inspection of witness statements and statements of case for accurate reporting after extensive press coverage.
The judge had to decide redaction of third-party names in the defendant's witness statement and whether further statements of case should be open to inspection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Mid-trial ruling on applications for inspection of witness statements under CPR 32.13 and statements of case under CPR 5.4.
enrichment.outcome: Mr Jones's witness statement ordered open to inspection with third-party names redacted to initials save one individual; particulars of claim and amended defence and counterclaim permitted for inspection; response to request for further information withheld.
enrichment.ratio: Witness statements standing as evidence in chief are generally open to inspection under CPR 32.13; the interests of justice may justify limited redaction of third-party identities where abandoned allegations would otherwise unfairly damage reputations, but allegations relevant to the jealousy issue should not be wholly excised.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 32.13 permits restriction on inspection of a witness statement confirmed in chief
Meaning of 'interests of justice' in CPR 32.13(3)(a)
Whether third-party names should be redacted where factual allegations were withdrawn
Extent of non-party access to statements of case under CPR 5.4

confidence.notes: Procedural ruling and CPR citations are explicit. Underlying property merits were not decided.

notes: Case stated appeal on section 78 exclusion where motorist refused blood specimen pending solicitor contact; Kennedy v DPP principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Failure to provide blood specimen: solicitor access and section 78 exclusion refused
key_facts: The appellant failed roadside and intoximeter breath tests at Stevenage Police Station and refused a required blood specimen, citing fear of needles and a wish to speak to a solicitor.
PC Emmerson did not enquire about solicitor availability during the specimen procedure but the duty solicitor was contacted about 20 minutes after the procedure ended.
Magistrates refused a section 78 application to exclude the blood procedure evidence and convicted the appellant of failing without reasonable excuse to provide a specimen.
The appeal challenged whether the officer's failure to consider facilitating solicitor contact required exclusion of evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Stevenage Magistrates' Court to the High Court (Administration).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; justices were correct to refuse exclusion under section 78 and to convict.
enrichment.ratio: Following Kennedy v DPP, a general request for legal advice during tightly regulated drink-drive specimen procedures does not require immediate delay to contact a solicitor where none is immediately available; any section 58 breach from later delay was neither significant nor substantial and did not render admission of the evidence unfair under section 78.
legal_issues: Whether police must delay section 7 specimen procedures to allow solicitor contact
Construction of section 58 PACE in drink-driving investigations
Whether failure to consider solicitor access amounted to a section 58 breach
Exercise of discretion under section 78 where Article 6 rights are engaged
linked_authorities: Ministry of Transport v Noort [1992] 3 NZLR 260

confidence.notes: Legal principles and outcome follow established Kennedy line clearly. Certificate for House of Lords was discussed but not finally decided.

notes: Long professional negligence trial on Wasps rugby ground valuation and Part 20 claim against solicitors; liability and quantum conclusions are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Wasps rugby club damages for negligent undervaluation of Sudbury ground
key_facts: Wasps Football Club trustees claimed damages from surveyors LSH over a March 1996 valuation of their Sudbury ground at £832,500 on a depreciated replacement cost basis.
Wasps transferred the ground at that valuation into a corporate structure linked to Christopher Wright and Loftus Road Plc as English rugby turned professional.

LSH admitted negligence in using DRC rather than open market value and in failing to make proper planning enquiries; a later DTZ valuation and residential planning permission showed substantially higher value.
LSH also pursued a Part 20 claim against Wasps' solicitors NGJ alleging failure to advise on retaining planning upside.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of claim for breach of contract and negligence against valuers, with Part 20 proceedings against solicitors.
enrichment.outcome: Wasps awarded £2,417,500 damages plus interest; contributory negligence and mitigation defences rejected; Part 20 claim against NGJ dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: LSH were negligent in valuing the ground on a DRC basis without adequate planning enquiries when an open market valuation of about £3.25m should have been reported; loss was the difference attributable to the undervaluation, and Wasps were not contributorily negligent in proceeding on the negligent advice.
legal_issues: Whether LSH breached duty in adopting DRC rather than open market valuation
Whether proper planning enquiries should have identified residential development potential
Assessment of counterfactual conduct and quantum of valuation loss
Whether Wasps were contributorily negligent or failed to mitigate
Whether NGJ owed duties to advise on retaining planning upside or correcting covenant references
linked_authorities: South Australia Asset Management Corp v York Montague Ltd [1997] AC 191

confidence.notes: Final damages figure and dismissal of Part 20 claim are clear. Detailed counterfactual and causation reasoning is extensive but coherent.

notes: Leading cohabitee beneficial interest appeal adjusting equal shares to 60/40; fair-share approach for unmarried couples is clearly articulated.

enrichment.short_title: Oxley v Hiscock: fair shares for unmarried cohabitees' home proceeds

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Mr Hiscock bought 35 Dickens Close in his sole name as a home for himself, Mrs Oxley, and her children after his return from captivity in Iraq.
The purchase was funded by a mortgage, proceeds of Mrs Oxley's former home at Page Close (partly funded by Mr Hiscock), and Mr Hiscock's savings.
The county court judge held the parties intended equal beneficial shares in the sale proceeds.
Mr Hiscock appealed, arguing his greater direct financial contribution made an equal split unfair.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Bromley County Court order under section 14 of TLATA 1996 determining shares in sale proceeds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Mrs Oxley held entitled to 40% and Mr Hiscock to 60% of proceeds; each party to bear own appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where unmarried cohabitees have no express agreement on beneficial shares and no communicated common intention at acquisition, the court should ask what fair share each should have regard to the whole course of dealing; equal shares may be unfair where one party's direct contribution to purchase price was substantially greater.
legal_issues: How to determine beneficial shares between unmarried cohabitees on separation
Role of common intention constructive trust versus resulting trust analysis
Whether equal sharing could be inferred from pooling of resources and conduct
Correct approach where no express discussion of shares occurred at purchase
linked_authorities: Lloyds Bank plc v Rosset [1991] 1 AC 107

confidence.notes: Appeal outcome and 60/40 split reasoning are explicit. Historical survey of cohabitee authorities is lengthy but the operative ratio is clear.

notes: Section 68 challenge to LCIA/UNCITRAL award on reply and affirmation points; Colman J's section 33 and issue-dealing analysis is detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Margulead v Exide: section 68 challenge to refusal of closing reply
key_facts: Margulead, an Israeli lead-extraction company, challenged an international arbitration award in favour of Exide under a pilot plant agreement governed by Georgia law.
The sole arbitrator declined counsel's request to reply orally to Exide's closing submissions and later upheld mutual mistake, rejecting Margulead's affirmation argument without detailed reasons.
Margulead applied under section 68 alleging serious irregularity causing substantial injustice on both the 'Reply Point' and 'Affirmation Point'.
The hearing procedure had been fixed in advance as one hour each for final speeches followed by a colloquy, not English-style last-word reply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996 to set aside an international arbitration award.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on both grounds; no serious irregularity under section 68 established.
enrichment.ratio: Denying a reply speech where procedure was agreed in advance and no novel points were raised did not breach section 33; failure to reason on an argument is not failure to deal with an 'issue' under section 68(2)(d), and any objection should have been raised forthwith under section 72.
legal_issues: Whether refusing oral reply to closing submissions breached section 33 fair opportunity duty
Whether arbitrator's silence on affirmation/waiver argument amounted to section 68(2)(d) failure to deal with an issue
Distinction between deficiency of reasons and failure to determine a claim or defence
Effect of section 72 waiver where procedural objection not raised promptly
linked_authorities: Hussman (Europe) Ltd v Al Ameen Development & Trade Co [2002] 2 Lloyd's Rep 83

confidence.notes: Both section 68 grounds are addressed comprehensively with clear dismissal. Affirmation point reasoning is alternative but fully reasoned.

notes: Edited trust variation judgment approving full capital advancement for minor beneficiary under Variation of Trusts Act 1958.

enrichment.short_title: Minor beneficiary: court approval to advance whole trust fund for education
key_facts: Proceeds of two life insurance policies were held on trust in equal shares for three minors including claimant C, aged 12.
Income and part of the capital had already been applied to C's school fees but were insufficient for future needs.
Section 32 limited advancement to half of C's presumptive share unless varied.
The court was asked to approve use of the whole capital for C's education and maintenance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Private paper application for court approval of trust variation on behalf of a minor beneficiary.
enrichment.outcome: Court approved variation permitting trustees to apply the whole of C's fund under section 32, not merely half.
enrichment.ratio: Property held on bare trust for an absolutely entitled minor falls within the Variation of Trusts Act 1958; lifting the section 32 half-limit is a permissible variation for the beneficiary's benefit where full advancement for education is justified.
legal_issues: Whether section 32 Trustee Act 1925 applies to a minor absolutely entitled to a separate fund
Whether the Variation of Trusts Act 1958 applies to bare trusts for minors
Whether the court could authorise advancement of the whole capital rather than half
Relationship between inherent Chancery jurisdiction and the 1958 Act
linked_authorities: Allen v Distillers Co (Biochemicals) Ltd [1974] QB 384

notes: TCC preliminary issues on PFI hospital M&E subcontract formation, repudiation, and HGCRA withholding notice; detailed findings on limited purchase orders.

enrichment.short_title: Emcor v Sir Robert McAlpine: Dudley PFI M&E subcontract preliminary issues

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: EDS (Emcor Drake and Scull) carried out mechanical and electrical works as subcontractor to SRM on the Dudley Hospitals PFI project after protracted negotiations for a £34.25m subcontract.
SRM issued serial limited purchase orders totalling £14m pending execution of a formal deed subcontract; EDS started work in July 2001 without returning an initial comfort letter.
The parties never executed a formal subcontract conforming with their August 2001 letter of understanding; SRM removed EDS from site in December 2002 alleging repudiatory breach.
EDS claimed £1,105,160.65 unpaid; SRM issued a section 111 withholding notice relying on alleged repudiation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of preliminary issues on contract scope, repudiation, and validity of a withholding notice.
enrichment.outcome: EDS not obliged to complete whole M&E works; contract limited to work under £14m orders; repudiation issue not decided; withholding notice unnecessary; payment order refused pending quantum hearing.
enrichment.ratio: The August 2001 letter was not a sufficiently certain synallagmatic contract for the entire works where key terms remained unresolved and no conforming subcontract was proffered; EDS worked under limited purchase orders up to £14m and was not in repudiatory breach merely by refusing an uncapped £34m order.
legal_issues: Whether a binding subcontract for all M&E works was concluded in August 2001
Whether EDS was obliged to complete the whole project or only work under limited orders
Whether EDS repudiated by refusing to work beyond accepted order limits
Whether SRM's section 111 withholding notice was necessary or effective
linked_authorities: Rupert Morgan Building Services Ltd v David Jervis [2004] BLR 18

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue answers are clearly listed. Repudiation and final quantum remain for later determination.

enrichment.short_title: Wiltshire v Powell: costs of second to fourth respondents on appeal
key_facts: The unsuccessful appellant Wiltshire resisted a costs order in favour of the second, third and fourth respondents.
Wiltshire argued those respondents had stood by without participating in the original action and that only Mr Powell was truly successful.
The Court of Appeal had held that Wiltshire's failure to join all relevant parties initially caused the second action.
The court also refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal ruling on costs following an unsuccessful appeal; application for leave to appeal further refused.
enrichment.outcome: Usual costs order made in favour of the second, third and fourth respondents; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where the appellant's own failure to bring all relevant parties before the court on the first occasion necessitated the second action, it is not unjust to award the usual costs on appeal to respondents who did not actively participate in the original proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether non-participating successful respondents should recover appeal costs
Effect of a party's failure to join necessary parties at first instance on costs allocation

notes: Costs Office preliminary issue on scope of LSC certificate limiting funding to appeal of 20 December 2001 costs enforcement order.

enrichment.short_title: Ryan v Dunscrest: scope of legal aid certificate on Court of Appeal costs
key_facts: Mr Ryan's leasehold claim against Dunscrest was struck out at trial and he was ordered to pay costs including £25,000 on account.
He appealed with LSC funding limited to challenging the 20 December 2001 costs enforcement order; merits grounds were refused permission.
The costs appeal was settled by consent quashing the on-account and enforcement orders.
Dunscrest sought determination of who bore liability for unfunded merits appeal costs and what costs protection applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supreme Court Costs Office preliminary issue on the scope of Community Legal Service funding certificates.
enrichment.outcome: Certificate held to cover only the application for permission to appeal the order made and dated 20 December 2001, not the substantive 14 November 2001 merits order.
enrichment.ratio: Where an LSC certificate limits funding to 'the order of 20 December 2001', it refers to the order actually made on that date concerning costs enforcement, not the wrongly dated substantive order of 14 November 2001; unfunded merits appeal costs fall outside costs protection under regulation 5(4) CLS Costs Protection Regulations 2000.
legal_issues: Construction of LSC funding certificate limitations
Whether merits and costs appeals were separately funded
Extent of section 11 AJA costs protection for partially funded proceedings
Liability as between assisted person and LSC for unfunded appeal costs
